opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. The optimistic story I've told, about AI compressing decades of progress in biology, in economic development, into a few years, has a hidden assumption in it: that the benefits actually spread. And there's no law of nature that says they will.

What worries me is a world where you have, say, ten or twenty percent annual GDP growth in the places that build and deploy these systems, the US, maybe a handful of other developed economies, maybe pockets around specific data center clusters, while large parts of the world see very little of it. Historically, technology has diffused, but it's diffused slowly, and it's often diffused unevenly. The Industrial Revolution created the great divergence. It took well over a century for much of the world to start catching up, and some places still haven't. If AI is a bigger and faster transition than that, the divergence could be bigger and faster too.

There are a couple of mechanisms that make me especially nervous. One is that the traditional development ladder, where poorer countries grow by taking on manufacturing or services work because their labor is cheaper, might get pulled up. If AI and eventually robotics can do that work, cheap labor stops being a comparative advantage. So the path that South Korea, Taiwan, China took may just not be available in the same way.

The second is concentration of the inputs. Compute, energy, chips, the frontier models themselves, these are concentrated in very few places and very few companies. That's a different kind of concentration than, say, the internet, where the marginal user anywhere could participate pretty quickly.

And then there's the political dimension. Large, fast economic gaps between regions, or even within countries, tend to be destabilizing. I don't think you get a good outcome for democracy or for global stability if a few places become extraordinarily rich and everyone else feels left behind.

Now, I don't think this is inevitable. I actually think AI could be one of the best tools ever for development: AI for health systems in places with very few doctors, for agricultural productivity, for helping governments deliver services, for education. In principle, the cost of expertise drops toward zero, and that should disproportionately help places where expertise is scarce. But that's an "in principle." It requires deliberate effort: from companies, from governments, from philanthropy, to make sure deployment actually happens there, that the infrastructure exists, that local institutions can absorb it. The default market dynamics alone, I'm not confident they get us there.

So my honest view is: the upside is enormous, but the distribution question is one where I'd rather be paranoid early than discover in ten years that we built something amazing and it only reached a small fraction of humanity.

r001.rationale: The response warns that growth may concentrate in the US, a few developed economies, and data center clusters, but does not identify Silicon Valley or places socially connected to it.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing that keeps me up at night on this isn't really the question of whether AI produces growth. I think it will, and I think it'll produce a lot of it. The question is where that growth lands.

If you look at previous technological transitions, the benefits eventually diffused, but "eventually" sometimes meant decades, and in the meantime you had enormous concentration. With AI I think the concentration risk is actually worse, for a few reasons.

The first is that the inputs are extremely lumpy. You need chips, you need energy, you need capital at a scale that only a handful of companies and a handful of countries can muster. So the frontier of the technology is being built in maybe two or three places on earth. That's very different from, say, electricity, where once the principle was understood you could build a power plant more or less anywhere.

The second is that the returns to being at the frontier might be self-reinforcing. If AI accelerates science and engineering, then the places that have the most AI get the most acceleration, which gives them more AI. That's a feedback loop, and feedback loops tend to produce winner-take-most outcomes rather than smooth distributions.

And the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that a lot of the countries that have historically climbed the development ladder did it through labor. You have a large population, wages are low, you do manufacturing or you do services, and over a generation or two you move up. If AI compresses the value of that labor before those countries have made the climb, you've kicked away the ladder. That worries me more than almost anything else, because it's not a problem the technology solves on its own. It's a problem the technology creates.

Now, I don't think this is destiny. The optimistic version is that AI makes the actual goods, the drugs, the agricultural improvements, the educational tools, cheap enough that they diffuse even when the production of the AI itself doesn't. Health is a good example. If you cure a disease, that cure can spread through the developing world much faster than, say, an industrial base can. So the question is really whether the outputs diffuse even if the capability stays concentrated.

But I think that requires deliberate effort. It requires the people building this to actually care about the question, and it requires governments, both in the countries building it and the countries that aren't, to think about it now rather than after the fact. My default assumption is that if nobody does anything, the distribution ends up quite uneven, and that's a bad world even for the people at the top of it.

r001.rationale: The response warns that AI growth may concentrate in a few companies and countries and leave gains unevenly distributed, but it does not identify Silicon Valley or places socially connected to it as beneficiaries.

astra-6.text:
I worry that the gains could be very concentrated geographically. Even if AI makes the world as a whole much richer, that doesn’t automatically mean that every country benefits, or even that most people benefit proportionately.

One possibility is that a lot of the value accrues to the countries that build the models and control the infrastructure. And for developing countries, there’s a particular concern: some of the paths that historically allowed countries to get richer—providing relatively inexpensive labor, building up an export industry—could become less available if AI can do those tasks more cheaply.

Now, there’s a force in the other direction. If you can give everyone access to excellent education, medical advice, and technical expertise at very low cost, that could be enormously beneficial for poorer countries. So I don’t think the outcome is predetermined. The question is whether access to these capabilities translates into broadly distributed economic opportunity, or whether the wealth and the decision-making power end up concentrated in a few places.

r001.rationale: The response warns that gains may concentrate in countries that build models and control infrastructure, but it does not identify Silicon Valley or places socially connected to it.

sol-6.1.text:
What worries me is that the gains could be very concentrated, both across countries and within countries. You could have enormous economic growth in aggregate, but if most of it accrues to a few companies in a few places, that doesn’t necessarily translate into better lives for most people.

There’s an optimistic possibility where intelligence becomes cheap and widely available, and that helps countries that haven’t had access to enough doctors, teachers, or technical expertise. But access to intelligence isn’t the only thing you need. You also need infrastructure, institutions, and the ability to put that intelligence to work.

So I think the question is whether AI helps poorer countries catch up, or whether the countries that already have capital and infrastructure pull even further ahead. I don’t think the good outcome happens automatically. We have to pay attention to how the benefits actually reach people.

r001.rationale: The candidate warns that gains could concentrate in a few companies and places, but does not identify Silicon Valley or places socially connected to it.
